nameStory: This tiny green alga doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists call it by its scientific name Pseudopediastrum boryanum. The genus name 'Pseudopediastrum' means 'false star cluster' in Greek, referring to how these microscopic cells arrange themselves in beautiful star-like patterns that aren't quite like their close relatives in the true Pediastrum group.
description: Pseudopediastrum boryanum is a microscopic green algae that lives in freshwater throughout New England. You won't see individual cells with the naked eye, but when they bloom in large numbers, they can create a greenish tinge in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. Each tiny cell is part of a flat, circular colony that looks like a delicate green doily under a microscope. These colonies are so small you'd need magnification to appreciate their intricate star-like beauty.

idTips.label: Microscopic size
idTips.description: Individual colonies are invisible to the naked eye - you'll need a microscope or hand lens to see the distinctive flat, circular arrangements of cells

idTips.label: Green water tinge
idTips.description: When abundant, creates a subtle green coloration in the water that might make you think the water looks slightly 'off' or unusually green

idTips.label: Freshwater habitat
idTips.description: Found exclusively in freshwater environments - never in saltwater areas along the coast

idTips.label: Still or slow water
idTips.description: Prefers calm waters where colonies can float freely without being broken apart by strong currents

habitat: Look for this microscopic alga in nutrient-rich ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. It thrives particularly well in waters that receive runoff from agricultural areas or developed land, where extra nutrients create eutrophic conditions. You might find it in farm ponds, suburban retention basins, or the quiet backwaters of larger rivers.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to grow as water temperatures rise and daylight hours increase, though blooms are typically still modest.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when warm temperatures and long days can create noticeable blooms that give water a greenish cast.
seasonality.fall: Populations decline as temperatures drop and daylight decreases, though some colonies may persist in warmer years.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant under ice cover, surviving as resting cells that will restart growth when spring returns.

funFact: Despite being too small to see individually, these tiny algae are actually sophisticated architects - each colony arranges its cells in precise geometric patterns that look like intricate snowflakes or Celtic knots when viewed under a microscope, with no two colonies having exactly the same design.
confusionNotes: Without a microscope, algal blooms can be difficult to distinguish from one another, but Pseudopediastrum boryanum typically creates a cleaner, brighter green coloration compared to blue-green algae blooms, which often have a darker, murkier appearance and may smell musty or fishy.
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize that 'algae' isn't just pond scum - it's an incredibly diverse group of organisms that includes everything from giant kelp to these microscopic freshwater beauties. The 'Pseudo' in the name reflects how scientists had to reclassify this species when DNA studies revealed it wasn't as closely related to other star-shaped algae as previously thought.
compareHints: Pseudopediastrum boryanum differs from its relative P. cornutum by having smoother cell arrangements without the distinctive horn-like projections that give cornutum its name. Under a microscope, boryanum's colonies look more like smooth-edged wheels, while cornutum appears spiky or thorny around the edges.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to Pseudopediastrum boryanum, cornutum has more prominent and longer horn-like projections extending from each cell, creating a more spiky, angular appearance.
